newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ pensions should continue in current form - Todd.
newsitem.headline: NZ pensions should continue in current form - Todd.

text.p: New Zealand's present tax- payer funded superannuation scheme is working well and should be maintained with some gradual changes, an interim report released on Thursday by the 1997 Periodic Report Group (PRG) said.
Commonly known as the Todd Taskforce, the PRG is an independent body set up by the government to monitor the retirement income system.
Its report concluded New Zealand Superannuation (NZS) was sustainable with some gradual changes to meet the demands placed on the scheme by an ageing population after 2015.
"The tide is coming in but it is not an unexpected or unpredictable tsunami," said Jeff Todd, the Auckland accountant chairing PRG.
"Careful preparation is needed but we don't need to dismantle what we have in place."
New Zealanders will vote in a postal referendum in September on whether to replace NZS with a compulsory pension scheme advocated by Treasurer Winston Peters.
Peters argues NZS is unsustainable, and earlier on Thursday predicted in parliament that the Todd Taskforce would reach the same conclusion.
However, Todd recommended NZS continue in its current form.
It said NZS (net of tax) currently cost about four percent of Gross Domestic Product each year.

"If NZS continues as it is now, but without the surcharge, net expenditure on NZS as a proportion of GDP will start to rise once baby boomers retire in increasing numbers around 2015, and reach about nine percent of GDP in 2050," the report said.
"We don't think this will create an economic crises though. Many other OECD countries are facing even stronger pressures on their public pension schemes."

PRG said there were a number of possible options for ensuring NZS stayed affordable, including raising the age of eligibility, and paying less publicly-provided superannuation to those who could provide for themselves in retirement.
Another option was continuing to increase NZS each year to cover inflation, but not linking it fully to average earnings, which tended to grow faster.
The report emphasised that any changes should be gradual.

The PRG said it regretted the planned abolition of the superannuation surcharge from April 1 next year, but it provided an opportunity to find a more acceptable way of linking public and private provision.
The PRG saw merit in establishing a standard individual rate of NZS independent of marital status.

The PRG will produce a final report by December 31, taking into account the result of the September referendum. The PRG was not required to assess the pros and cons of the government's proposed compulsory superannuation scheme.
